title: How Is Automated Research Evaluated?A Survey of Benchmarks and Evaluation Practices

paper.title: How Is Automated Research Evaluated? A Survey of Benchmarks and Evaluation Practices
paper.abstract: Abstract Automated research systems support literature synthesis, ideation, experiments, writing, and peer review, but their evaluation is dispersed across tasks, benchmarks, and studies that are difficult to compare directly. We review this literature from the perspective of evaluation design and evidence, covering six targets: literature synthesis, research ideation, executable workflows, scholarly writing and communication, automatic peer review, and end-to-end research. We compare task construction, evidence sources, evaluators, and scoring procedures to explain the capabilities assessed by different designs. Our synthesis highlights three recurring lessons: output checks, process checks, and human studies provide complementary information; evaluator calibration is specific to the property being assessed; and resource budgets and attempt selection are integral to interpreting performance comparisons. We identify diagnostic evaluation designs and documented gaps in supporting evidence, and translate these comparisons into reporting and audit recommendations for specific evaluation settings. The survey helps readers navigate existing evaluations, select appropriate benchmarks, and design subsequent studies.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Research agents search papers, formulate proposals, run experiments, write, and review manuscripts. Correct computations, useful literature comparisons, and supported criticisms require different observations. Interpreting their benchmark scores therefore requires understanding the task, available evidence, and scoring procedure. Existing surveys and perspectives organize automated research around the scientific method, workflow stages, autonomy, applications, and system architectures ( Zhang et al., 2025a ; Luo et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2025c ; Zheng et al., 2025 ; Wei et al., 2025 ; Xie et al., 2025 ; Ren et al., 2026 ) . Our review brings together the evaluation literature within this landscape: benchmarks, datasets, execution environments, human studies, metrics, and audit protocols. We compare their experimental designs as well as reported scores. Across six evaluation targets, we distinguish questions requiring different evidence, such as a review’s usefulness to its author versus its detection of a known error. Figure 1 maps representative works by target and claims supported by their core evaluation designs. The survey makes three contributions. First, it organizes and reviews evaluation studies , explaining their tasks and assessment procedures. Second, it compares evaluation designs and synthesizes findings , connecting evidence, scoring, and calibration to assessed capabilities and support gaps. Third, it develops setting-specific recommendations for benchmark selection, result interpretation, and evaluation design. The appendix records protocols and reporting details.

sections.heading: 2 Scope and Review Method
sections.text: We review evaluation of automated research workflows, their artifacts, and human interaction through explicit tasks or inspectable scoring procedures. Standalone retrieval, single-paper question answering, generic coding, and autonomous wet-lab systems are outside the main coverage; selected adjacent tasks contribute distinctive designs to core comparisons.

sections.heading: Search and selection.
sections.text: We searched Google Scholar, arXiv, Semantic Scholar, and the ACL Anthology iteratively alongside writing, with backward and forward citation tracing. The cutoff was May 10, 2026; descriptions of some studies incorporate subsequent revisions. Queries combined target and evaluation terms (Appendix B ). This selective review places representative comparisons in the main text and additional designs and details in the appendix. Cross-target studies are classified by their primary evaluation question.

sections.heading: Analysis fields.
sections.text: We compare the target (capability, artifact, or stage), evidence source (judgment materials and observations), evaluator (person, model, or procedure), metric (scoring and aggregation), and validity boundary (applicability conditions and identified claim–evidence gaps). Evidence-source analysis considers both provenance and support for output judgments. Related RAG studies examine evidence-based output calibration ( Chen et al., 2025a ) and multi-granularity retrieval for verification ( Chen et al., 2026 ) . We use these fields to check evidence and scoring against authors’ stated claims, distinguish observations from proxies, and examine calibration, identifying conclusions supported under the reported conditions. Five claim-strength levels organize interpretation. L1: Surface plausibility concerns artifact style or appearance. L2: Task correctness under specified evidence concerns success under defined inputs and checks. L3: Process-grounded competence requires criterion-checked process evidence explaining execution or decisions, beyond stored logs. L4: Human- or utility-calibrated performance relates results to defined populations’ judgments or outcomes, distinguishing preference, factual assessment, and practical benefit. L5: Scientific contribution concerns advances supported by domain-appropriate novelty, methods, results, interpretation, and validation. Cross-stage interpretation separates local results, verified overall completion, and stage interactions; process records explain interactions but are not universally required for reporting observable final outcomes.

sections.heading: Classifying representative works.
sections.text: Figure 1 classifies core evaluation designs and main experiments; supplementary process analyses, human ratings, and scorer audits do not independently determine placement. Works without a single-level summary of equally central designs are omitted. Table and Appendix B detail selected classifications and protocols. Figure 1: Representative works by claim strength. Highlighted hexagon segments indicate primary evaluation targets. AstaBench (E2E) denotes only the suite’s end-to-end component. Level 5 indicates a direction for further evaluation development. Most selected works assess task correctness (L2). BLADE, AstaBench (E2E), and MLR-Bench check analysis decisions or research steps (L3); RE-Bench and Scideator center expert-performance or user-judgment comparisons (L4).

sections.heading: 3 Target-Specific Evaluation
sections.text: We compare representative task designs and synthesize findings and open questions, interpreting specific protocols and reported results.

sections.heading: 3.1 Scientific Literature Synthesis Evaluation
sections.text: Literature synthesis turns multiple papers into an organized account of a research area or an answer to a research question. Evaluation must therefore specify who selects the sources, what the system produces, and how that output is checked. Long surveys, comparison tables, taxonomies, and question-driven answers expose different parts of this task; they are complementary evaluation settings, not successive stages of a single benchmark.

sections.heading: Survey generation and content assessment.
sections.text: AutoSurvey retrieves papers, builds an outline, and writes and revises individual sections ( Wang et al., 2024 ) . Its evaluation separates citation support from coverage, structure, and relevance. Importantly, its citation recall measures support among sentences already containing citations, rather than recovery of a human bibliography. SurGE instead uses 205 human surveys and a shared retrieval pool to compare reference coverage, citation accuracy, structure, and content ( Su et al., 2026 ) . Its expert ranking study calibrates structure and content scores; it does not validate the separate citation judgments, which use titles and abstracts. Thus, similarly named citation metrics can have different denominators and evidence access. SurveyGen makes another important condition explicit: its 120-survey experiment distinguishes topic-only generation, automatic retrieval, and writing with human-provided references and outlines ( Bao et al., 2025 ) . The last condition tests writing with supplied organization, not autonomous source selection.

sections.heading: Structured synthesis.
sections.text: Comparison tables require choosing useful dimensions and filling them with paper-specific evidence. ArxivDIGESTables evaluates these operations separately: schema recall measures recovery of human comparison columns, while cell evaluation supplies the human schema to isolate information extraction ( Newman et al., 2024 ) . Human checks cover 50 tables for column alignment and 30 for cell matching. Additional context mainly improves partial cell matches; generated columns absent from the reference are not significantly less useful in the reported study. Reference recovery and usefulness are therefore separately observable. TaxoBench similarly distinguishes finding expert-cited papers from organizing a supplied paper set into a hierarchy ( Zhang et al., 2026b ) . Its reported structural controls show that semantic path scores respond strongly to tree depth and category wording, so raw alignment differences require interpretation alongside these controls.

sections.heading: Question-driven synthesis and information use.
sections.text: OpenScholar evaluates citation-bearing scientific answers using expert questions, rubrics, and preferences; its expert comparison covers 108 questions and 16 evaluators ( Asai et al., 2024 ) . ResearchQA scales a related task by mining questions and scoring requirements from surveys across 75 fields, with expert validation in eight fields ( Yifei et al., 2025 ) . These designs differ in how information needs are obtained and how widely human calibration extends. SurveyBench instead asks whether an already generated survey supplies the information needed for general and topic-specific quizzes ( Sun et al., 2025 ) . Across 20 topics, an LLM answers from retrieved survey passages, and unsupported answers receive zero. DeepResearch scores 4.42/5 on content but 1.97/10 on topic-specific questions; LLM × \times MapReduce-V2 scores 4.20 and 3.19, respectively. This reversal shows why content ratings and supported answerability should both be inspected. DeepSurvey-Bench adds a rubric for information, scholarly communication, and research guidance ( Zhang et al., 2026a ) . It reports human calibration on 40 generated surveys and a separate evidence audit sampled from high-scoring surveys. That audit describes evidence quality within the selected group. More generally, Hwang et al. (2026) find that system-level agreement with experts can conceal weaker instance-level agreement in scientific long-answer evaluation.

sections.heading: Synthesis.
sections.text: The most informative designs separate source selection, organization, and use. Shared retrieval pools and supplied-outline conditions help identify which part of the task a comparison tests. Separate schema and cell evaluations similarly make an unsuccessful table easier to diagnose. ArxivDIGESTables’ useful non-reference columns motivate assessing alternative structures alongside reference alignment; SurveyBench’s differing content and answerability rankings show why covered information must also be usable for answering questions. Evaluation should match intended use: coverage and organization for field overviews, supported answerability for questions, and citation checks with explicit evidence access and denominators for source-grounded claims. Calibration must follow these distinctions. Expert agreement on content, structure, or preference does not validate separate citation or individual-answer scoring. Reporting these dimensions separately would reveal which component accounts for a system’s strengths or failures.

sections.heading: 3.2 Research Ideation and Proposal Evaluation
sections.text: Research ideas are evaluated before their proposed experiments have produced results. Novelty asks how an idea differs from existing work; feasibility concerns whether its steps can be carried out; value concerns the expected importance of the contribution. Existing protocols approach these questions through expert judgments, comparison with published ideas, retrieved prior work, and evidence-bearing proposal reports.

sections.heading: Expert judgments and published references.
sections.text: Si et al. (2024) compare human ideas, automatically selected AI ideas, and human-reranked AI ideas in seven prompting-based NLP topics. Their study involves 104 distinct researchers and 49 proposals per condition, with blinded ratings after style normalization. At the idea level, AI proposals receive higher novelty scores than human proposals, while feasibility differences are not significant. This is a comparison of the specified generation and selection processes: AI uses extensive sampling and retrieval, whereas each human contributes one idea. AI Idea Bench asks a different question ( Qiu et al., 2025 ) . It supplies inspiration papers and a topic for 3,495 target papers, then evaluates generated motivations and experimental plans through target-paper matching and pairwise comparisons. Topic alignment, recovery of a published idea, and expert-perceived novelty consequently have different reference objects, even when all are used to evaluate ideation.

sections.heading: Novelty relative to prior work.
sections.text: Literature-Grounded Novelty Assessment makes the comparison set explicit ( Shahid et al., 2025 ) . It retrieves candidate papers, reranks them by purpose, mechanism, evaluation, and application, and judges novelty against the top ten using expert examples. On 32 held-out ideas, its reported accuracy is 0.81 and agreement with expert labels is κ = 0.59 \kappa=0.59 . A separate 58-case study tests only known non-novel ideas and should not be read as overall classification accuracy. Navigating Ideation Space instead separates problem, method, and findings representations, providing component-level links to prior work ( Shen et al., 2026 ) . Its novelty score correlates with 93 expert-rated ideas, but the reported Spearman correlation of 0.384 is close to GPT-5 Mini’s 0.385. Scideator brings related facet-based reasoning into an interactive tool ( Radensky et al., 2026 ) . Its user study finds higher creativity-support ratings from 22 researchers, measuring tool experience rather than expert novelty labels.

sections.heading: Feasibility and proposal feedback.
sections.text: AI Idea Bench also derives overall and per-step feasibility proxies from the normalized, time-weighted citation impact of papers linked to decomposed idea steps. The authors interpret the per-step score as methodological soundness. However, citation impact does not test whether a retrieved method applies to the present step or whether steps are compatible; independent calibration against step-feasibility judgments is not reported. These scores directly measure the influence of associated literature. ScholarEval and InnoEval seek richer assessments by producing evidence-bearing feedback ( Moussa et al., 2026 ; Qiao et al., 2026 ) . ScholarEval separates soundness and contribution analysis, evaluates coverage of 1,076 expert-checked feedback requirements, and studies report usefulness with 18 researchers. InnoEval combines papers, web resources, and code with multiple simulated reviewer perspectives; it evaluates historical decision labels, rankings, and expert dimension scores.

sections.heading: Synthesis.
sections.text: Ideation evaluation is most interpretable when novelty, feasibility, and feedback usefulness remain distinct. Blinding and style normalization control presentation; links to prior literature expose the basis of novelty judgments; expert-feedback requirements make coverage observable. These designs support interpretation without requiring agreement with a single published idea. The unresolved feasibility question is whether influential supporting literature establishes that the current plan is implementable. AI Idea Bench’s citation-derived proxies provide evidence about the associated papers. Its per-step methodological-soundness interpretation lacks calibration against method applicability and step compatibility. Such judgments would test the proposed connection between its citation-derived proxies and feasibility. Practitioners could combine literature-grounded novelty assessment with separately calibrated feasibility judgments and feedback-usefulness studies. Expert comparisons should also report generation and selection budgets, which determine the proposals reaching evaluators.

sections.heading: 3.3 Executable Research Workflow and Scientific Coding Evaluation
sections.text: Executable workflow evaluation covers scientific calculations, data analysis, and machine-learning research engineering. Systems receive tasks and computational resources and return code, predictions, or analysis outputs. Running these artifacts enables direct checks, but the checks differ: successful execution, correct scientific outputs, defensible analysis decisions, and improved experimental performance are distinct targets.

sections.heading: Scientific code and analysis.
sections.text: SciCode uses scientist-curated problems with numerical and domain-specific tests ( Tian et al., 2024 ) . Its 65-problem test set contains 288 subproblems, allowing local implementations and their integration to be compared. Claude 3.5 Sonnet solves 26.0% of subproblems but 4.6% of main problems in the standard setting; supplied scientific background raises these to 35.4% and 12.3%. These conditions help diagnose knowledge and integration requirements. Because experts provide the decomposition, the results test implementation along that workflow rather than the system’s ability to invent the decomposition. ScienceAgentBench moves to self-contained Python programs for 102 data-driven scientific tasks ( Chen et al., 2025d ) . It separates valid execution from task-specific success, using numerical checks, prediction thresholds, and, for some visual outputs, model scoring. For Claude’s self-debugging configuration without expert knowledge, valid execution reaches 92.2%, but task success is 32.4%, under best-of-three selection. BLADE instead evaluates choices among defensible analyses: conceptual variables, data transformations, and statistical models are matched to expert reference decisions ( Gu et al., 2025 ) . Its finding that executable analyses can still cover few reference decision combinations illustrates what a run/no-run check misses. DiscoveryBench scores final hypotheses by matching their conditions, variables, and relationships ( Majumder et al., 2024 ) . Its no-data baseline is diagnostic: Llama-3 scores 11.5 without data versus 12.1 with CodeGen. This identifies a contribution from question and metadata information; the matching score alone does not isolate data verification.

sections.heading: Machine-learning engineering and research methods.
sections.text: MLE-bench packages 75 Kaggle competitions as offline tasks ( Chan et al., 2025 ) . Given a description and data, agents train models and submit predictions to a local hidden-test grader. Historical private-leaderboard thresholds translate task scores into medal attainment. Under AIDE, a 24-hour budget, and one A10 GPU, o1-preview attains a medal threshold in 16.9% of attempts; allowing eight attempts raises the at-least-one-success rate to 34.1%. Runtime and hardware specify conditions, while contamination checks audit the evidence. Because many tests are resplit from original training data, historical medals are calibrated references: the authors check example solutions and acknowledge that reconstructed and original competitions are not exactly equivalent. RE-Bench supplies a complementary human comparison: 61 experts make 71 eight-hour attempts in seven research-engineering environments ( Wijk et al., 2025 ) . Relative performance changes with the budget. The reported 32-hour human result selects the best of four independent eight-hour attempts, rather than observing one continuous 32-hour session. This design makes time and attempt allocation explicit parts of the comparison. MLRC-Bench connects proposed methods to implemented results in seven research competitions ( Zhang et al., 2025b ) . Agents modify a protected repository, select a snapshot on development performance, and undergo hidden-test evaluation. Scores normalize improvement relative to baseline and human solutions and can be negative. Its auxiliary o1 novelty ratings have Spearman correlation − 0.06 -0.06 with measured effectiveness. Under this protocol, perceived innovativeness is a poor predictor of competition performance; effectiveness is not itself a novelty label, so the correlation does not establish that novelty judgments are inaccurate.

sections.heading: Synthesis.
sections.text: Executable evaluation gains diagnostic value by separating running code, obtaining correct results, and making appropriate analysis decisions. SciCode’s local and integrated tests and ScienceAgentBench’s execution and success measures locate different failures. BLADE checks analysis decisions against expert alternatives. DiscoveryBench’s no-data control shows why performance must also be examined against information available without execution. Figure 1 distinguishes task checks (L2), direct analysis-decision evaluation (L3), and RE-Bench’s controlled expert comparison (L4). For research engineering, hidden-test scores provide an endpoint, while attempt selection, feedback, and compute define its conditions. MLE-bench and RE-Bench show why best-of-several outcomes and single-attempt success answer different operational questions. Comparisons should preserve both task success and resource cost. Decision-level checks add evidence about how an analysis was conducted. Their role depends on whether the intended use is output verification, workflow diagnosis, or performance comparison under a shared budget.

sections.heading: 3.4 Academic Writing and Scholarly Communication Evaluation
sections.text: Scientific writing evaluation asks whether a system expresses research accurately, uses sources appropriately, and communicates through a particular medium. These questions require different observations: reconstructing a citation paragraph, checking a reference, and reading a poster are distinct tasks. Their shared concern is how information survives selection, attribution, and presentation.

sections.heading: Source-supported writing.
sections.text: CiteBench standardizes citation-sentence and paragraph generation from supplied papers and citing context ( Funkquist et al., 2023 ) . It combines reference similarity with citation-intent and discourse distributions, and human ratings of readability and consistency. In its 150-output human study, average consistency remained below 3/5 across models, despite readable outputs. Reference reconstruction also depends on input sufficiency: the authors document targets containing facts absent from the permitted input, although the affected proportion is unquantified. Thus, some reconstruction errors cannot be attributed solely to the generator. At introduction level, SciIG separately evaluates reference-set recovery, content, and narrative quality from supplied metadata ( Garg et al., 2026 ) . The results show that its keyword-overlap measures and human factuality judgments have weak alignment, illustrating why metric names alone do not establish what they measure. Task manipulation helps explain these differences. Across two models, six prompts, and six input configurations, Sahinuç et al. (2024) vary abstracts, citation intent, and example citations. Their exploratory 30-example human study finds that automatic measures provide only partial agreement with atomic-fact coverage. Reference-derived intent is an explicit experimental input, allowing the study to examine how task definition changes output. GREP instead evaluates related-work sections against hard constraints, such as source support, and soft preferences, such as citation emphasis and positioning ( Şahinuç et al., 2026 ) . Its protocol includes 16 NLP/CV experts and criterion-specific comparisons. An initial 20% faithfulness pass rate for o3-mini means that every citation passed in 20% of sections, not that only 20% of citations were faithful. Reported citation-format parsing failures also enter this score, so it does not isolate semantic reasoning failures.

sections.heading: Reference and citation verification.
sections.text: Bibliographic validity and contextual support need different evidence. BibAgent retrieves source passages to diagnose miscitation; its paywall setting instead uses downstream citing papers as indirect evidence and can abstain ( Li et al., 2026 ) . MisciteBench contains 6,350 expert-checked synthetic miscitations, all erroneous. Its Acc-pass@3 requires a correct validity label and an accepted explanation in at least one of three attempts; it therefore does not estimate false alarms on naturally correct citations. CiteAudit tests existence and metadata consistency on separate generated and real-world collections containing valid and invalid references ( Shi et al., 2026 ) . Its reported precision falls from .947 to .749 while recall remains .971 and .951, respectively. Separate confusion matrices expose differences that a single accuracy or synthetic-data result would conceal.

sections.heading: Visual communication.
sections.text: Paper2Poster’s PaperQuiz asks six vision-language models to answer source-paper questions using only a poster ( Pang et al., 2025 ) . This measures information accessibility alongside visual and textual quality; raw answer accuracy is separate from its length-adjusted score. Human calibration involved one PhD participant and five papers, limiting evidence for a general human-reader proxy. PaperBanana instead compares method diagrams on faithfulness, conciseness, readability, and aesthetics, with a hierarchical overall judgment ( Zhu et al., 2026 ) . Separate 50-example studies calibrate the judge and collect blind preferences. Its overall improvement coexists with faithfulness below the reference baseline.

sections.heading: Synthesis.
sections.text: Writing evaluation becomes actionable when criteria identify revision needs. GREP separates unsupported content from unwanted emphasis or presentation choices. Citation-generation findings show that reference-based errors must be interpreted against the writer’s inputs; separating parsing from semantic verification would likewise distinguish formatting failures from support failures. These distinctions help turn an overall writing score into a diagnosis that can guide revision. Readability, faithfulness, and information access can diverge, as SciIG’s weak metric–human alignment and PaperBanana’s differing overall and faithfulness results illustrate. Reference verification additionally requires detecting errors without false alarms on valid references. Assessment should therefore combine criteria suited to the artifact and its readers: source support and author constraints for prose, and fidelity and information accessibility for visual summaries. Human calibration should test the particular reader judgment represented by each automated measure.

sections.heading: 3.5 Automatic Peer Review Evaluation
sections.text: A useful scientific review connects criticism to manuscript evidence and gives its recipient something interpretable or actionable. Evaluation accordingly examines review content, the validity of specific criticisms, and effects within the review process. The central design choice is which property the available reference or observation can check.

sections.heading: Review content and evaluator calibration.
sections.text: ReviewEval decomposes quality into alignment with human reviews, factual accuracy, analytical depth, constructiveness, and guideline adherence ( Garg et al., 2025 ) . Its factuality pipeline converts comments into questions, retrieves manuscript passages, generates a rebuttal, and checks support. Five experts also compare anonymous reviews on 30 papers, but their four preference dimensions do not supply independent labels for that question-level verifier. Consequently, high automatic support rates have different evidential backing from the reported human preferences. Peerispect makes verification explicit through supported, partially supported, contradicted, and undetermined labels ( Ghorbanpour et al., 2026 ) . Its constructed manuscript-claim set contains only supported claims; the separate real-review set supplies the multi-class test. GEM addresses another evaluator question: how much information a review shares with independent peer references when no unique gold review exists ( Xu et al., 2025 ) . Teacher-score correlations and ICLR review-degradation tests are separate experiments. GEM is sensitive to information removal; unlike GPT-4o LMExaminer, its scores do not significantly increase after meaningless expansion in those tests. However, it does not outperform the LLM judge on every calibration measure.

sections.heading: Criticism and error localization.
sections.text: Natural weaknesses and controlled errors offer complementary reference construction strategies. CLAIMCHECK links expert-selected weaknesses to manuscript claims and separates claim association, weakness labeling/editing, and claim verification ( Ou et al., 2025 ) . Labeling/editing supplies the weakness; verification does not. The performance difference between these settings makes the input distinction essential. FLAWS constructs claim-invalidating edits and evaluates ranked error locations in 713 paper–error pairs ( Xi et al., 2025 ) . Its top-k score uses candidate depth within one output, with length restrictions on proposed spans. Human inspection validates 57 of 58 sampled errors, while a separate comparison checks automatic detection judgments. This provides evidence about both the constructed problems and their scorer. SPOT instead contains 91 author-acknowledged errors in 83 historical manuscripts ( Son et al., 2025 ) . Models receive interleaved text and images; their descriptions are matched to known errors, and repeated runs support pass@K estimates. However, expert case analysis identifies a genuine unit error outside the annotations. Since unmatched findings count as false positives, matching precision cannot directly estimate the factual reliability of every criticism. PRISMM-Bench further isolates cross-modal inconsistencies through identification, remedy selection, and visual matching ( Selch et al., 2026 ) . Focused, page, and document contexts distinguish local recognition from broader inspection; no-context and structured-option controls reveal how answer wording can support guessing.

sections.heading: Usefulness and workflow effects.
sections.text: RevUtil evaluates author-oriented actionability, grounding/specificity, verifiability, and helpfulness using 1,430 human-annotated review points ( Sadallah et al., 2025 ) . Its scorer sees the comment, not the paper: grounding means pointing to manuscript content, while verifiability concerns supplied reasons. A randomized ICLR deployment observes a different endpoint by providing feedback to reviewers after submission ( Thakkar et al., 2025 ) . Of 22,467 reviews assigned to feedback, 18,946 received it after gating. Review edits and discussion behavior are measured separately from blind preferences on 100 selected high-uptake revision pairs. The reported 89% preference for revisions concerns that subset.

sections.heading: Synthesis.
sections.text: Peer-review evaluation combines three views: complete-review quality, criticism correctness, and feedback effects. Multidimensional assessment, controlled or historical errors, and utility or deployment studies provide complementary evidence about content, detection, and use. Controlled errors make detection and localization testable, while historical errors retain problems encountered in real manuscripts. Human-annotated utility criteria and randomized deployment connect content to recipient judgments and workflow behavior. No single reference set supplies all three. Calibration must match the scored property. A preference study assesses perceived review quality; an automated factuality checker needs independent judgments of manuscript support. ReviewEval illustrates this distinction, while FLAWS separately validates constructed errors and detection judgments. SPOT’s valid finding outside its annotations shows why unmatched criticism needs adjudication before matching precision can represent factual reliability. Workflow studies add practical effects, but conclusions remain tied to feedback assignment, receipt, and the preference-study subset. Combining these checks would evaluate useful, well-grounded reviews while keeping content assessment, factual verification, and workflow effects separately interpretable.

sections.heading: 3.6 End-to-End Automatic Scientific Research System Evaluation
sections.text: End-to-end research evaluation follows a connected sequence of research decisions and outputs. The sequence depends on the task: some systems start with code templates, others with a research question or dataset. A multi-task suite may include such sequences alongside isolated tasks. Understanding the starting resources and final success criterion is therefore necessary before comparing overall scores.

sections.heading: Systems and evaluation environments.
sections.text: The AI Scientist connects ideation, experiments, figures, writing, and automated review within lightweight ML templates ( Lu et al., 2024 ) . Its counts of proposed ideas, completed experiments, and compiled papers expose different failure points. DeepScientist studies sustained exploration from reproduced baselines, combining task-native improvements, implementation records, and expert assessments ( Weng et al., 2025 ) . Its reported results include human verification and substantial compute. These examples motivate reusable protocols while retaining each system’s starting points and verification arrangements. AstaBench provides 11 benchmarks spanning literature, code, analysis, and end-to-end discovery, with tool and cost metadata ( Bragg et al., 2026 ) . The suite’s aggregate is not a single connected research run. Its E2E-Bench and Hard variant evaluate reports, code, and artifacts against required research steps. A step passes only when evidence does not conflict and at least one source supports completion. The original study’s Table 21 reports that 16% of rubric-criterion assessments appeared satisfied in the paper but were contradicted by code or artifacts. Separately, a human spot check judged 92% of 50 development-set rubric scores to be correct. Mean step scores and all-required-step completion are reported separately; the non-executing Faker control receives partial step credit but completes no whole task. Cross-artifact checks thus identify inconsistencies that report-only evaluation would miss.

sections.heading: Research artifacts and executable outcomes.
sections.text: MLR-Bench uses workshop-derived open research questions and phase-specific rubrics ( Chen et al., 2025b ) . Its 201 tasks support idea and proposal evaluation, whereas experiments, writing, and end-to-end runs mainly use ten selected tasks. MLR-Judge averages two model assessments and inspects execution records as well as papers. The authors report unverified synthetic or placeholder-data results in eight of ten Claude Code tasks, a concrete reason to inspect execution. Ten experts provide calibration, but non-significant differences between human–model and human–human score discrepancies do not establish statistical equivalence. ResearchGym supplies runnable repositories with source methods removed, retained baselines, and task-native graders ( Garikaparthi et al., 2026 ) . Under the initial 12-hour, single-A100 and $10 API budget, its main agent improves on the strongest visible baseline in one of 15 runs; mean subtask completion is 26.5%. Reporting completion, improvement, and best@3 separately distinguishes reliable execution from occasional gains. AIRS-Bench supplies data and evaluation scripts without initial solution code, accepting prediction files for hidden-label scoring ( Lupidi et al., 2026 ) . Its 24-hour, single-H200 repeated runs offer a contrasting starting condition, so results should be compared through both task design and resource settings.

sections.heading: Rediscovery and stage diagnosis.
sections.text: FIRE-Bench asks agents to recover established empirical findings while withholding the original implementation and conclusions ( Wang et al., 2026 ) . For example, a question about information position can target the finding that relevant evidence is used better at the beginning or end of context than in the middle. The study runs 30 core and ten cross-domain problems, not the entire 100-paper source pool. Atomic-claim precision, recall, and F1 compare conclusions with reference findings; trajectory inspection attributes errors to planning, implementation, execution, and conclusion formation. Its added human check validates claim extraction, not the entire subsequent entailment scorer.

sections.heading: Synthesis.
sections.text: End-to-end evaluation needs explicit starting resources, required stages, and success criteria. Supplied templates, runnable baselines, and data-only starting points impose different research demands. Reporting stage and whole-task completion identifies where connected runs stop; hidden-test performance or reference-finding recovery measures their outcomes. Comparisons should retain these distinctions rather than assume equivalent starting points. Cross-artifact verification makes completion judgments more diagnostic. AstaBench’s report–artifact disagreements and MLR-Bench’s placeholder-data cases show that code and experimental records can change the assessment of an apparently completed report. Process inspection tests whether claimed steps occurred and helps attribute failures; its findings should remain distinct from primary outcome scores, as with rediscovery matching and trajectory analysis. Evaluations should report starting assistance, verified completion, task-native outcomes, and resource use together, retaining successful runs and failures rather than only an aggregate artifact score.

sections.heading: 4 Toward Credible Evaluation Infrastructure
sections.text: The comparisons motivate task-dependent reporting (Table ): input-sufficiency issues in CiteBench, the need for feasibility-proxy calibration in AI Idea Bench, problem and scorer checks in FLAWS, and report–artifact verification in AstaBench.

sections.heading: Comparability and calibration.
sections.text: Resource conditions and repeated attempts shape results: MLE-bench varies attempt budgets, and RE-Bench compares agents and experts at stated time budgets. Long-software-task research provides background on task duration and success measurement ( Kwa et al., 2025 ) . Evaluators also need checks: general LLM-judge studies document position and verbosity biases and examine possible self-enhancement bias ( Zheng et al., 2023 ) . Their occurrence and impact require verification in each scientific setting.

sections.heading: Reporting recommendations.
sections.text: Report the task and intended claim, inputs and data version, evaluator and scoring, sample and aggregation unit, and applicability conditions. Combine applicable modules in Table , such as error construction and matching for localization, or participants and outcomes for feedback utility. Public artifacts support inspection and reuse.

sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: Across six targets, this survey compares evaluation designs, synthesizes findings and evidence gaps, and develops setting-specific reporting recommendations. These comparisons help readers select benchmarks, interpret results, and design subsequent evaluations.

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.text: This review is selective and emphasizes automated research workflows in AI/ML with inspectable evaluation evidence. It does not exhaust the broader AI-for-Science or autonomous wet-lab literature. Coverage is also uneven across disciplines because many available benchmarks concern computer science and machine learning. We synthesize reported studies and documented protocols rather than independently reproducing their experiments. The five claim distinctions guide interpretation; they are not a validated measurement scale or an exhaustive taxonomy of scientific value.

sections.heading: Appendix A Comparative Mapping and Reporting Recommendations
sections.text: Table summarizes selected applications of the claim-strength analysis. Table records the task-dependent reporting recommendations discussed in Section 4 .

sections.heading: Appendix B Search and Protocol Records
sections.text: The following tables document protocols within the review’s six targets, including the studies discussed in the main text. Rows distinguish task inputs, the evidence used to judge outputs, scoring, calibration or controls, and findings or applicability conditions. Multiple protocols from one work are distinguished when their evidence or scoring differs. Search terms combined each target with evaluation-related variants. Literature synthesis queries included survey generation, cross-paper comparison, and survey evaluation; ideation queries included research idea evaluation and novelty assessment; workflow queries included scientific code, data analysis, and ML research agents. Writing queries included citation-text generation, citation support, and scientific communication artifacts; reviewing queries included grounded critique, error localization, and review utility; end-to-end queries included research agents, research environments, and scientific rediscovery. Backward and forward citation tracing connected these searches. The tables preserve relevant alternative designs rather than all neighboring application areas.

sections.heading: B.1 Scientific Literature Synthesis Protocols
sections.text: The protocols below distinguish survey generation, structured synthesis, and question-driven information use. Separate rows identify different scoring tasks within a work; human reference artifacts and independent human judgments are recorded separately.

sections.heading: B.2 Research Ideation and Proposal Protocols
sections.text: Expert judgments, published-paper references, literature-relative novelty, and proposal feedback use different labels. The table separates assessment of ideas from assessment of interactive support or report usefulness.

sections.heading: B.3 Executable Workflow and Scientific Coding Protocols
sections.text: These protocols inspect scientific functions, analysis decisions, program outputs, or machine-learning improvements. Execution tests, model judgments, and process measurements remain separate; resource and feedback conditions specify how each result was obtained.

sections.heading: B.4 Academic Writing and Scholarly Communication Protocols
sections.text: The records separate source-supported prose and aspect-level scoring, bibliographic validity and contextual citation support, and visual communication. Separate rows distinguish protocols within one work; calibration samples are not counted as additional works.

sections.heading: B.5 Automatic Peer Review Protocols
sections.text: The records distinguish review-content evaluators, manuscript-grounded criticism, multimodal checking, and feedback use or aggregation. Natural weaknesses, injected errors and decision labels supply different references; a paper may therefore contribute several task-specific rows.

sections.heading: B.6 End-to-End Research Protocols
sections.text: System demonstrations and review-feedback studies are followed by multi-task infrastructure, connected research subprotocols, and rediscovery. The suite, stage and full-run rows preserve their different denominators.

Wong † † thanks: Equal contribution. † † thanks: Corresponding author. NLPCT Lab Department of Artificial IntelligenceUniversity of Macau, Macau, China Email: nlp2ct.{liulei,chuyue,guanhua,yutong}@gmail.com Email: {mc55091,lidiasc,cmvong,derekfw}@um.edu.mo Abstract Automated research systems support literature synthesis, ideation, experiments, writing, and peer review, but their evaluation is dispersed across tasks, benchmarks, and studies that are difficult to compare directly. We review this literature from the perspective of evaluation design and evidence, covering six targets: literature synthesis, research ideation, executable workflows, scholarly writing and communication, automatic peer review, and end-to-end research. We compare task construction, evidence sources, evaluators, and scoring procedures to explain the capabilities assessed by different designs. Our synthesis highlights three recurring lessons: output checks, process checks, and human studies provide complementary information; evaluator calibration is specific to the property being assessed; and resource budgets and attempt selection are integral to interpreting performance comparisons. We identify diagnostic evaluation designs and documented gaps in supporting evidence, and translate these comparisons into reporting and audit recommendations for specific evaluation settings. The survey helps readers navigate existing evaluations, select appropriate benchmarks, and design subsequent studies. 1 Introduction Research agents search papers, formulate proposals, run experiments, write, and review manuscripts. Correct computations, useful literature comparisons, and supported criticisms require different observations. Interpreting their benchmark scores therefore requires understanding the task, available evidence, and scoring procedure. Existing surveys and perspectives organize automated research around the scientific method, workflow stages, autonomy, applications, and system architectures ( Zhang et al., 2025a ; Luo et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2025c ; Zheng et al., 2025 ; Wei et al., 2025 ; Xie et al., 2025 ; Ren et al., 2026 ) . Our review brings together the evaluation literature within this landscape: benchmarks, datasets, execution environments, human studies, metrics, and audit protocols. We compare their experimental designs as well as reported scores. Across six evaluation targets, we distinguish questions requiring different evidence, such as a review’s usefulness to its author versus its detection of a known error. First, it organizes and reviews evaluation studies , explaining their tasks and assessment procedures. Second, it compares evaluation designs and synthesizes findings , connecting evidence, scoring, and calibration to assessed capabilities and support gaps. Third, it develops setting-specific recommendations for benchmark selection, result interpretation, and evaluation design. Analysis fields. We compare the target (capability, artifact, or stage), evidence source (judgment materials and observations), evaluator (person, model, or procedure), metric (scoring and aggregation), and validity boundary (applicability conditions and identified claim–evidence gaps). Evidence-source analysis considers both provenance and support for output judgments. Related RAG studies examine evidence-based output calibration ( Chen et al., 2025a ) and multi-granularity retrieval for verification ( Chen et al., 2026 ) . We use these fields to check evidence and scoring against authors’ stated claims, distinguish observations from proxies, and examine calibration, identifying conclusions supported under the reported conditions. Five claim-strength levels organize interpretation. L1: Surface plausibility concerns artifact style or appearance. L2: Task correctness under specified evidence concerns success under defined inputs and checks. L3: Process-grounded competence requires criterion-checked process evidence explaining execution or decisions, beyond stored logs. L4: Human- or utility-calibrated performance relates results to defined populations’ judgments or outcomes, distinguishing preference, factual assessment, and practical benefit. L5: Scientific contribution concerns advances supported by domain-appropriate novelty, methods, results, interpretation, and validation. Cross-stage interpretation separates local results, verified overall completion, and stage interactions; process records explain interactions but are not universally required for reporting observable final outcomes.
